<script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w02">{"year":1,"week":2,"id":"y1w02","title":"Properties of Operations and Sets","subtitle":"The closure, commutative, associative and distributive laws, identities and inverses — and the language of subsets, unions and intersections.","family":"number","section":{"no":1,"name":"Number","strand":"Number for Everyday Life","from":1,"to":8},"outcomes":["State and test the commutative, associative and distributive laws for real numbers.","Use a counterexample to show that a general statement is false.","Use identities, inverses and the distributive law to simplify and solve.","Use the words subset, union, intersection and complement, and draw simple Venn diagrams."],"keywords":["operation","property","closure","commutative","associative","distributive","identity","inverse","reciprocal","subset","union","intersection"],"notes":[{"title":"Operations and properties","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"An **operation** is a rule that combines two numbers to give a result. The four familiar operations are addition $(+)$, subtraction $(-)$, multiplication $(\\times)$ and division $(\\div)$."},{"k":"p","text":"A **property** is a general rule about an operation that is true for **every** allowed choice of numbers. Addition is an operation; the statement $a+b=b+a$ is a property of addition. Knowing the properties tells us when we may reorder, regroup or simplify a calculation without changing its value."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Closure and counterexamples","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Closure","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A set $S$ is **closed** under an operation $\\ast$ if, for every $a$ and $b$ in $S$, the result $a\\ast b$ is also in $S$."}]},{"k":"p","text":"Whole numbers are closed under $+$ and $\\times$ but not under $-$ or $\\div$. Integers are closed under $+$, $-$ and $\\times$. Rational and real numbers are closed under all four operations, provided we never divide by zero."},{"k":"p","text":"To show a set is **not** closed, name the set and find one pair whose result falls outside it. For $S=\\{1,2,3\\}$, even addition is not closed: $2+3=5\\notin S$. A small set does not inherit the closure of the integers."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"One counterexample is enough","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A single example that works does not prove a statement about every number. A single **counterexample** proves the statement false."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"The commutative law — changing the order","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For all real numbers $a$ and $b$:"},{"k":"math","tex":"a+b=b+a\\qquad\\text{and}\\qquad ab=ba"},{"k":"p","text":"For example, $14+26=26+14=40$ and $(-3)\\times8=8\\times(-3)=-24$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w02-arrays","caption":"Turning an array of 3 rows of 4 on its side gives 4 rows of 3: the total is 12 either way, so $3\\times4=4\\times3$."},{"k":"p","text":"Subtraction and division are **not** commutative: $8-3=5$ but $3-8=-5$; $12\\div3=4$ but $3\\div12=\\dfrac{1}{4}$. When you explain why a law fails, show both results."}],"figs":["w02-arrays"]},{"title":"The associative law — changing the grouping","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For all real numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$:"},{"k":"math","tex":"(a+b)+c=a+(b+c)\\qquad\\text{and}\\qquad(ab)c=a(bc)"},{"k":"p","text":"The brackets move but the numbers stay in the same order. For example, $(20+35)+45=20+(35+45)=100$, and the second grouping is quicker because $35+45=80$."},{"k":"p","text":"Subtraction and division are **not** associative:"},{"k":"math","tex":"(12-5)-2=5\\quad\\text{but}\\quad 12-(5-2)=9"},{"k":"math","tex":"(24\\div6)\\div2=2\\quad\\text{but}\\quad 24\\div(6\\div2)=8"},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Do not mix up the two laws","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **commutative** law changes the **order** of the numbers. The **associative** law changes only the **grouping** (the brackets)."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"The distributive law","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Multiplication distributes over addition and subtraction:"},{"k":"math","tex":"a(b+c)=ab+ac\\qquad\\qquad a(b-c)=ab-ac"},{"k":"p","text":"Every term inside the bracket is multiplied by the factor outside: $4(3x-5)=12x-20$, **not** $12x-5$. A negative factor changes every sign: $-2(3x-7)=-6x+14$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w02-area","caption":"The area of the whole rectangle, $5(x+3)$, equals the sum of the two parts, $5x+15$."},{"k":"p","text":"**Factorising** reverses the distributive law: $18x+24=6(3x+4)$. It is useful for mental arithmetic, for example $25\\times48+25\\times52=25(48+52)=25\\times100=2500$."}],"figs":["w02-area"]},{"title":"Identity and inverse elements","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Identities and inverses","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["The **additive identity** is $0$, because $a+0=0+a=a$.","The **multiplicative identity** is $1$, because $a\\times1=1\\times a=a$.","The **additive inverse** of $a$ is $-a$, because $a+(-a)=0$.","The **multiplicative inverse** (reciprocal) of a non-zero number $a$ is $\\dfrac{1}{a}$, because $a\\times\\dfrac{1}{a}=1$."]}]},{"k":"p","text":"The additive inverse of $-\\dfrac{11}{5}$ is $\\dfrac{11}{5}$. The reciprocal of $-\\dfrac{4}{7}$ is $-\\dfrac{7}{4}$, because $\\left(-\\dfrac{4}{7}\\right)\\left(-\\dfrac{7}{4}\\right)=1$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w02-inverse","caption":"A number and its additive inverse are the same distance from 0 on opposite sides, so they add up to 0."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Zero has no reciprocal","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"There is no number $x$ with $0\\times x=1$, because $0\\times x$ is always $0$. That is why $\\dfrac{a}{b}$ is undefined when $b=0$."}]}],"figs":["w02-inverse"]},{"title":"Properties in algebra, and the language of sets","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The laws work together when we simplify. For $25(4x+3)-3(25x+2)$, expand each bracket and then regroup like terms:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\begin{aligned}&25(4x+3)-3(25x+2)\\\\&=100x+75-75x-6\\\\&=(100x-75x)+(75-6)\\\\&=25x+69\\end{aligned}"},{"k":"p","text":"When solving, keep both sides balanced: from $3(x+2)=12$, divide **both** sides by 3 to get $x+2=4$, so $x=2$."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Set vocabulary","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["$A\\subseteq B$ ($A$ is a **subset** of $B$): every element of $A$ is also in $B$.","$A\\subset B$ ($A$ is a **proper subset** of $B$): $A\\subseteq B$ and $A\\neq B$.","$A\\cup B$ (**union**): elements in $A$ or in $B$ or in both.","$A\\cap B$ (**intersection**): elements in both $A$ and $B$.","$A'$ (**complement**, also written $A^{c}$): elements of the universal set $U$ that are not in $A$."]}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w02-subset","caption":"$A=\\{2,4\\}$ lies inside $B=\\{2,4,6\\}$, and $B$ has the extra element 6, so $A\\subset B$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w02-venn","caption":"Survey of Worked Example 2.6: the numbers show how many learners are in each region."},{"k":"p","text":"These ideas lead to the three-set problems of Week 3."}],"figs":["w02-subset","w02-venn"]}],"examples":[{"title":"Laws of addition in a bank calculation","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"An account manager receives GH₵125, GH₵375 and GH₵625 in one day. Show how the associative law makes the total easy to find, and explain why $125-375$ does not obey the commutative law."}],"steps":["The total is $125+375+625$.","Regroup using the associative law: $(125+375)+625=125+(375+625)$.","$375+625=1000$, so the total is $125+1000=1125$.","For subtraction, $125-375=-250$ but $375-125=250$. The results differ, so subtraction is not commutative."],"answer":"Total GH₵1 125; addition is associative, subtraction is not commutative.","figs":[]},{"title":"The distributive law in a stationery order","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A school buys 18 packs of exercise books. Each pack holds 12 ruled books and 8 unruled books. Use the distributive law to find the total number of books."}],"steps":["Each pack holds $(12+8)$ books, so the total is $18(12+8)$.","Distribute: $18\\times12+18\\times8=216+144=360$.","Check the other way: $18\\times20=360$ ✓."],"answer":"360 books","figs":[]},{"title":"Solving with a negative coefficient","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Solve $-3(2x-5)+4(x+2)=13$ and check your answer."}],"steps":["Expand: $-3(2x-5)=-6x+15$ and $4(x+2)=4x+8$.","Combine: $-6x+15+4x+8=13$, so $-2x+23=13$.","Subtract 23 from both sides: $-2x=-10$.","Divide both sides by $-2$: $x=5$.","Check: $-3(10-5)+4(5+2)=-15+28=13$ ✓."],"answer":"$x=5$","figs":[]},{"title":"Additive and multiplicative inverses","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"For $a=-\\dfrac{3}{8}$, find the additive inverse and the multiplicative inverse, and check each one."}],"steps":["Additive inverse: we need $b$ with $a+b=0$. Since $-\\dfrac{3}{8}+\\dfrac{3}{8}=0$, $b=\\dfrac{3}{8}$.","Multiplicative inverse: turn the fraction upside down and keep the sign: $c=-\\dfrac{8}{3}$.","Check: $\\left(-\\frac{3}{8}\\right)\\left(-\\frac{8}{3}\\right)=\\frac{24}{24}=1$"],"answer":"Additive inverse $\\dfrac{3}{8}$; multiplicative inverse $-\\dfrac{8}{3}$.","figs":[]},{"title":"Is division associative?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A learner says division is associative because $(64\\div8)\\div2$ and $64\\div(8\\div2)$ use the same three numbers. How many are in at least one club?","options":["$39$","$27$","$33$","$9$"],"correct":1,"explain":"$18+15-6=27$: the 6 learners in both clubs are counted once."},{"q":"If $A=\\{2,4\\}$ and $B=\\{2,4,6\\}$, which statement is true?","options":["$B\\subset A$","$A\\cap B=\\varnothing$","$A\\subset B$","$A=B$"],"correct":2,"explain":"Every element of $A$ is in $B$, and $B$ has the extra element 6, so $A$ is a proper subset of $B$."}],"exercise":[{"q":"Show by calculation that $\\dfrac{4}{7}\\times\\left(-\\dfrac{3}{2}\\right)=\\left(-\\dfrac{3}{2}\\right)\\times\\dfrac{4}{7}$.","a":"Both products equal $-\\dfrac{12}{14}=-\\dfrac{6}{7}$."},{"q":"Solve $5(2x-3)-2(x+4)=17$ and check your answer.","a":"$10x-15-2x-8=17$, so $8x=40$ and $x=5$. The order of the elements does not matter, and repeating an element does not change the set: $\\{2,2,4\\}=\\{2,4\\}$."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Key terms","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["The **universal set** $U$ is the whole group being studied, for example all the learners in a class.","The **empty set** $\\varnothing$ has no elements, so $n(\\varnothing)=0$.","The **cardinality** $n(A)$ is the number of distinct elements in $A$."]}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Union, intersection, difference and complement","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For $A=\\{1,2,3\\}$ and $B=\\{3,4,5\\}$:"},{"k":"ul","items":["The **union** $A\\cup B=\\{1,2,3,4,5\\}$ contains the elements in $A$, in $B$ or in both. In mathematics “or” includes “both”.","The **intersection** $A\\cap B=\\{3\\}$ contains only the elements common to both sets.","The **difference** $A\\setminus B=\\{1,2\\}$ contains the elements of $A$ that are not in $B$. In general $A\\setminus B\\neq B\\setminus A$.","The **complement** $A'$ (also written $A^{c}$) contains the elements of $U$ that are not in $A$. If also $A\\neq B$, then $A$ is a **proper subset**, written $A\\subset B$. For example $\\{4,6\\}\\subset\\{2,4,6\\}$, while $\\{2,4,6\\}$ is a subset of itself but not a proper subset."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Counting subsets","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The empty set is a subset of every set. Exactly two: $8+10+6=24$.","Check: $36+24+4=64$, and $36+29+31-12-14-10+4=64$ ✓."],"answer":"Exactly one: 36; exactly two: 24.","figs":[]},{"title":"Verifying De Morgan’s law by listing","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Let $U=\\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8\\}$, $A=\\{1,2,3,5\\}$ and $B=\\{3,4,5,7\\}$. Describe $(A\\cup B\\cup C)'$ in words and explain why it equals $A'\\cap B'\\cap C'$."}],"steps":["$A\\cup B\\cup C$ is everyone taking at least one of the three subjects.","Its complement is everyone taking **none** of them.","To take none, a learner must be outside $A$ **and** outside $B$ **and** outside $C$.","“And” means intersection, so this set is $A'\\cap B'\\cap C'$."],"answer":"Both describe the learners who take none of Agriculture, Biology or Chemistry.","figs":[]},{"title":"A survey with all regions given","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A school surveyed 150 learners about three clubs. 40 joined $A$ only, 25 joined $B$ only, 20 joined $C$ only; 15 joined $A$ and $B$ only, 10 joined $A$ and $C$ only, 12 joined $B$ and $C$ only, and 8 joined all three. How many joined no club?"}],"steps":["These seven regions do not overlap, so add them.","One club only: $40+25+20=85$. Two clubs only: $15+10+12=37$.","Inside the circles: $85+37+8=130$.","No club: $150-130=20$. All eight regions now total 150 and none is negative ✓."],"answer":"20 learners","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results for Week 3","items":["A set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets and $2^n-1$ proper subsets.","$n(A\\cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\\cap B)$","$n(A\\cup B\\cup C)=n(A)+n(B)+n(C)-n(A\\cap B)-n(A\\cap C)-n(B\\cap C)+n(A\\cap B\\cap C)$","$(A\\cup B)'=A'\\cap B'$ and $(A\\cap B)'=A'\\cup B'$","“None” $=n(U)-n(A\\cup B\\cup C)$"]}],"quiz":[{"q":"If $A=\\{1,2\\}$ and $B=\\{1,2,3\\}$, which statement must be true?","options":["$A=B$","$B\\subset A$","$A\\subset B$","$A\\cap B=\\varnothing$"],"correct":2,"explain":"Every element of $A$ is in $B$, and $B$ has the extra element $3$, so $A$ is a proper subset of $B$."},{"q":"For $A=\\{1,3,5\\}$ and $B=\\{3,4,5\\}$, $A\\cap B$ is","options":["$\\{3,5\\}$","$\\{1,3,4,5\\}$","$\\{1,4\\}$","$\\varnothing$"],"correct":0,"explain":"The intersection contains only the elements in both sets: $3$ and $5$."},{"q":"A set with 4 elements has how many subsets?","options":["$4$","$8$","$12$","$16$"],"correct":3,"explain":"A set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets: $2^4=16$."},{"q":"Which expression is equal to $(A\\cup B\\cup C)'$?","options":["$A'\\cup B'\\cup C'$","$A'\\cap B'\\cap C'$","$A\\cap B\\cap C$","$A'\\cap(B\\cup C)$"],"correct":1,"explain":"De Morgan’s law takes the complement of every set and changes the union into an intersection."},{"q":"In a survey, $n(A)=30$, $n(B)=25$ and $n(A\\cap B)=12$. Find $n(A\\cup B)$.","options":["$67$","$43$","$55$","$13$"],"correct":1,"explain":"$n(A\\cup B)=30+25-12=43$."},{"q":"9 learners join all three clubs and 22 join both $A$ and $B$. How many are in $A$ and $B$ only?","options":["$31$","$22$","$9$","$13$"],"correct":3,"explain":"$n(A\\cap B)$ includes the 9 in all three clubs, so $A\\cap B$ only $=22-9=13$."},{"q":"The set $A\\setminus B$ contains the elements","options":["in $A$ but not in $B$","in either $A$ or $B$","in both $A$ and $B$","outside both $A$ and $B$"],"correct":0,"explain":"The difference $A\\setminus B$ keeps the elements of $A$ that are not in $B$."},{"q":"Three sets have sizes 30, 27 and 25; their pairwise intersections have sizes 8, 9 and 7, and the triple intersection has size 3. The union has size","options":["$61$","$58$","$64$","$76$"],"correct":0,"explain":"$30+27+25-8-9-7+3=82-24+3=61$."},{"q":"Which description means “in exactly two of $A$, $B$ and $C$”?","options":["$(A\\cup B\\cup C)'$","$A\\cap B\\cap C$","the three “two sets only” regions together","$A\\cup B\\cup C$"],"correct":2,"explain":"Exactly two means in two sets but not the third: the $A\\cap B$ only, $A\\cap C$ only and $B\\cap C$ only regions."},{"q":"$U$ has 80 members and $n(A\\cup B\\cup C)=68$. How many members are in none of the sets?","options":["$148$","$68$","$12$","$0$"],"correct":2,"explain":"None $=n(U)-n(A\\cup B\\cup C)=80-68=12$."}],"exercise":[{"q":"For $U=\\{1,2,\\ldots,12\\}$, $A=\\{2,4,6,8,10,12\\}$ and $B=\\{3,6,9,12\\}$, find $A\\cup B$, $A\\cap B$, $A'$ and $B'$.","a":"$A\\cup B=\\{2,3,4,6,8,9,10,12\\}$; $A\\cap B=\\{6,12\\}$; $A'=\\{1,3,5,7,9,11\\}$; $B'=\\{1,2,4,5,7,8,10,11\\}$."},{"q":"180 learners were asked about French, ICT and Economics: 90, 75 and 65 take them; 35 take French and ICT, 30 French and Economics, 25 ICT and Economics; 15 take all three. Find how many take exactly one, exactly two, at least one, and none.","a":"Exactly one 95, exactly two 45, at least one 155, none 25."},{"q":"Explain, in words, why $(A\\cup B\\cup C)'=A'\\cap B'\\cap C'$.","a":"An element outside $A\\cup B\\cup C$ is in none of the sets, so it is outside $A$, outside $B$ and outside $C$ — that is, in $A'\\cap B'\\cap C'$; the reverse is also true."},{"q":"A three-set Venn diagram has 6 in the centre, 7, 9 and 11 in the “two sets only” regions, and 14, 18 and 12 in the “one set only” regions. Find $n(A\\cup B\\cup C)$.","a":"$6+27+44=77$"},{"q":"How many proper subsets does a set with five elements have? Why is this one fewer than the number of subsets?","a":"$2^5-1=31$; the only subset that is not proper is the set itself."},{"q":"$n(A)=12$, $n(B)=9$ and $n(A\\cup B)=17$. Find $n(A\\cap B)$.","a":"$12+9-17=4$"},{"q":"List all the subsets of $\\{p,q,r\\}$.","a":"$\\varnothing$, $\\{p\\}$, $\\{q\\}$, $\\{r\\}$, $\\{p,q\\}$, $\\{p,r\\}$, $\\{q,r\\}$, $\\{p,q,r\\}$ — 8 subsets."},{"q":"In a group of 60 people, 35 like tea, 30 like coffee and 12 like both. How many like neither?","a":"$35+30-12=53$ like at least one, so $60-53=7$ like neither."}],"theory":[{"q":"Out of 100 learners, 52 take French $(F)$, 46 take ICT $(I)$ and 35 take Economics $(E)$; 20 take $F$ and $I$, 17 take $F$ and $E$, 14 take $I$ and $E$, and 7 take all three. Find all eight regions of the Venn diagram.","steps":["Centre: 7.","$F\\cap I$ only $=20-7=13$; $F\\cap E$ only $=17-7=10$; $I\\cap E$ only $=14-7=7$.","$F$ only $=52-13-10-7=22$; $I$ only $=46-13-7-7=19$; $E$ only $=35-10-7-7=11$.","Union $=22+19+11+13+10+7+7=89$; none $=100-89=11$."],"answer":"22, 19, 11, 13, 10, 7, 7 inside the circles and 11 outside.","model":null},{"q":"Let $U=\\{a,b,c,d,e,f\\}$, $A=\\{a,b,d\\}$ and $B=\\{b,c,f\\}$. Find $(A\\cup B)'$ and $A'\\cap B'$, and comment.","steps":["$A\\cup B=\\{a,b,c,d,f\\}$, so $(A\\cup B)'=\\{e\\}$.","$A'=\\{c,e,f\\}$ and $B'=\\{a,d,e\\}$, so $A'\\cap B'=\\{e\\}$.","The two sets are equal, as De Morgan’s law states."],"answer":"Both equal $\\{e\\}$.","model":null},{"q":"A survey reports 20 in $A$ only, 25 in $B$ only, 15 in $C$ only, 10 in $A\\cap B$ only, 6 in $A\\cap C$ only, 9 in $B\\cap C$ only and 5 in all three. How many chose exactly one, exactly two and at least two?","steps":["Exactly one: $20+25+15=60$.","Exactly two: $10+6+9=25$.","At least two: $25+5=30$."],"answer":"60, 25 and 30.","model":null},{"q":"Find the number of subsets and of proper subsets of a set with 6 elements. Explain the role of the empty set.","steps":["Each element is either included or not: $2^6=64$ subsets.","Only the set itself is not a proper subset: $64-1=63$ proper subsets.","The empty set is one of the 64 subsets, and it is a proper subset because the set is not empty."],"answer":"64 subsets and 63 proper subsets.","model":null},{"q":"Explain the three-set inclusion–exclusion formula, and why the triple intersection is added back after the pairs are subtracted.","steps":["Adding $n(A)+n(B)+n(C)$ counts an element in two sets twice and an element in three sets three times.","Subtracting the three pairwise intersections corrects the double counts, but an element in all three sets is subtracted three times, leaving a count of $3-3=0$.","Adding $n(A\\cap B\\cap C)$ once restores that element to a count of 1."],"answer":"Every element ends up counted exactly once.","model":null}],"checklist":["I can tell a subset from a proper subset and count subsets with $2^n$.","I can find unions, intersections, differences and complements.","I can fill in all eight regions of a three-set Venn diagram.","I can use the inclusion–exclusion formula for two and three sets.","I can state and check De Morgan’s laws."],"plan":{"lessons":[[{"j":0,"notes":true,"exs":[]},{"j":1,"notes":true,"exs":[0]},{"j":2,"notes":true,"exs":[1]},{"j":3,"notes":true,"exs":[]}],[{"j":4,"notes":true,"exs":[2,3]},{"j":5,"notes":true,"exs":[4,5]},{"j":6,"notes":true,"exs":[6]}]],"exSec":[1,2,4,4,5,5,6],"quizSec":[2,1,2,5,5,3,1,1,3,3],"exerSec":[5,4,3,3,2,5,2,1],"thSec":[3,1,4,2,4],"sumSec":[2,5,5,5,3],"chkSec":[2,1,3,4,5],"weights":[590.6,1486.4,1491.5,1262.1,2079.15,2294.9,1187],"figs":[{"id":"w03-subsets","sec":2,"lesson":1,"caption":"The set $\\{a,b,c\\}$ has $2^3=8$ subsets, including $\\varnothing$ and the set itself."},{"id":"w03-demorgan","sec":5,"lesson":2,"caption":"Shading the complement of the union leaves only the outside region;
